# The Inner Structure of Constituent Quarks in the Chiral Quark Model

In the chiral quark model ($\XQM$), the fundamental degrees of freedom governing the low-energy dynamics of hadrons are constituent quarks and Goldstone bosons. A central feature of this framework is that a constituent quark can emit Goldstone bosons, a process that reflects the spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry in quantum chromodynamics. Importantly, the flavor symmetry breaking that characterizes this emission process serves as a key ingredient for interpreting the observed flavor-spin structure of the nucleon. By encoding the differing probabilities for emitting Goldstone bosons of distinct flavors, the model provides a natural explanation for the empirical asymmetries found in the nucleon's internal composition.

In this paper, we investigate the inner structure of constituent quarks as it is implied by the chiral quark model. Specifically, we focus on the internal structure that emerges from the Goldstone boson emission process taking place within the nucleon. Rather than treating the constituent quark as a structureless point-like object, we examine how the dynamics of Goldstone boson emission endow the constituent quark with a nontrivial intrinsic structure.

To this end, the intrinsic wave functions of the constituent quarks are determined from a simplified model Hamiltonian that is derived from the chiral quark model. This simplified Hamiltonian retains the essential physics of the Goldstone boson emission process while remaining tractable, thereby allowing us to extract the relevant wave functions in a controlled manner.

The transition probabilities for Goldstone boson emission from a quark, obtained through this approach, are found to provide a reasonable interpretation of the flavor symmetry breaking that governs the nucleon's flavor-spin structure. This consistency between our results and the established phenomenology lends support to the physical picture underlying the chiral quark model and highlights the role of the intrinsic quark structure in accounting for the observed properties of the nucleon.

# The Chiral Quark Model and the Inner Structure of Constituent Quarks

## Introduction

The Chiral Quark Model (χQM) has emerged as a valuable theoretical framework for understanding the internal flavor-spin structure of the nucleon. At its core, the model is built upon the fundamental idea that constituent quarks are not simple point-like particles but possess an inner structure that manifests through their interactions with Goldstone bosons. In this picture, a constituent quark can emit a Goldstone boson—such as a pion, kaon, or eta meson—transforming into a quark of different flavor in the process. Crucially, this emission occurs with flavor symmetry breaking, a feature that proves essential for reproducing the experimentally observed properties of the nucleon.

## Motivation and Approach

The primary aim of this investigation is to probe the inner structure of the constituent quark itself. Rather than treating the constituent quark as an elementary object, we regard it as a composite system whose intrinsic properties can be described by a wave function. To this end, we derive these intrinsic wave functions starting from a simplified model Hamiltonian. This Hamiltonian is constructed to capture the essential physics of quark–Goldstone boson coupling while remaining tractable enough to yield explicit solutions.

By solving for the intrinsic states of the constituent quark within this framework, we obtain a description of how the quark's internal degrees of freedom are organized. These intrinsic wave functions encode the probability that a given constituent quark will emit a particular Goldstone boson, thereby linking the abstract Hamiltonian to physically measurable quantities.

## Results and Interpretation

From the derived wave functions, we compute the transition probabilities associated with the emission of the various Goldstone bosons. These probabilities are of central importance because they directly govern the degree of flavor symmetry breaking in the model. Since the different Goldstone bosons carry distinct masses—reflecting the underlying breaking of chiral symmetry—the emission rates for pions, kaons, and eta mesons differ accordingly. This mass hierarchy naturally translates into a hierarchy of transition probabilities.

The results demonstrate that the calculated transition probabilities provide a reasonable and physically consistent interpretation of the flavor symmetry breaking observed in the nucleon's flavor-spin structure. In particular, the suppression of emissions involving heavier Goldstone bosons, relative to the lighter pion, mirrors the pattern of symmetry breaking required to describe nucleon properties. This agreement lends support to the χQM picture and suggests that the internal structure of constituent quarks, as captured by the simplified Hamiltonian, offers a meaningful account of the mechanisms underlying flavor symmetry breaking.

## Conclusion

In summary, by deriving the intrinsic wave functions of constituent quarks from a simplified model Hamiltonian within the Chiral Quark Model, we are able to compute Goldstone boson emission probabilities that shed light on the inner structure of these quarks. The resulting transition probabilities successfully reproduce the essential features of flavor symmetry breaking in the nucleon, reinforcing the value of the χQM as a tool for understanding the interplay between quark substructure and the flavor-spin dynamics of hadrons.

# The Chiral Quark Model (XQM) and Goldstone Bosons

The chiral quark model, often abbreviated as XQM (or χQM), represents an important theoretical framework in particle physics for understanding the internal structure and dynamics of hadrons. It bridges the gap between the fundamental theory of the strong interaction—quantum chromodynamics (QCD)—and the observed properties of protons, neutrons, and other composite particles built from quarks.

## The Role of Goldstone Bosons

At the heart of the XQM lies the concept of the **Goldstone boson**. According to Goldstone's theorem, whenever a continuous symmetry of a physical system is spontaneously broken, massless (or nearly massless) particles known as Goldstone bosons emerge. In the context of QCD, the approximate chiral symmetry of the light quarks is spontaneously broken, giving rise to the pseudoscalar mesons—such as the pions, kaons, and the eta meson—which behave as the associated (pseudo-)Goldstone bosons.

Because these particles are not perfectly massless (the underlying symmetry is only approximate), they are more precisely called **pseudo-Goldstone bosons**, acquiring small masses from the finite quark masses.

## How the Model Works

In the chiral quark model, the effective degrees of freedom at low and intermediate energies are the constituent quarks and the Goldstone bosons themselves. Quarks interact by exchanging these Goldstone bosons, providing an intuitive picture of how the strong force manifests within hadrons. This approach has proven remarkably successful in explaining:

- The **spin and flavor structure** of the nucleon.
- The **"proton spin puzzle"**, which challenged naive quark models.
- Various **magnetic moments** and low-energy hadronic properties.
- Aspects of **flavor symmetry breaking** in the sea-quark distribution.

## Significance

The XQM demonstrates the power of combining symmetry principles with effective descriptions of matter. Rather than solving the full complexity of QCD directly—a formidable task at low energies—the model captures the essential physics through the interplay of constituent quarks and Goldstone bosons. This makes it a valuable and enduring tool for theorists seeking intuitive yet quantitatively meaningful insights into the world of subatomic particles.

# Abstract

We investigate the internal structure of constituent quarks within the framework of the chiral quark model (χQM), where the spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry endows current quarks with a dynamically generated mass and gives rise to Goldstone boson degrees of freedom. In this picture, a constituent quark is treated as a composite object consisting of a valence current quark surrounded by a cloud of pseudoscalar Goldstone bosons (π, K, η) generated through emission and reabsorption processes. We derive the effective quark-Goldstone boson coupling from the underlying chiral Lagrangian and compute the probability amplitudes for single- and multiple-boson fluctuations, characterizing the resulting spin, flavor, and momentum distributions carried by the constituent quark. Particular attention is paid to how Goldstone boson emission redistributes angular momentum between the valence quark core and the meson cloud, providing a natural mechanism for the observed suppression of the quark spin contribution to the nucleon spin ("proton spin puzzle") and the flavor asymmetry of the light-quark sea. We evaluate the constituent quark mass and its scale dependence, together with the intrinsic transverse-momentum structure induced by the boson cloud, and compare our predictions with experimental data on the Gottfried sum rule violation, semi-inclusive deep-inelastic scattering, and octet baryon magnetic moments. Our results demonstrate that the χQM with dynamical Goldstone boson emission offers a consistent and predictive description of low-energy hadron phenomenology, bridging the gap between the fundamental QCD Lagrangian and the effective constituent quark picture.

By reducing the full chiral Lagrangian to an effective two-body Hamiltonian, we compute the constituent quark's mass, size, and internal momentum distribution.
